 PORTLAND (WGME) -- A significant refund is coming to all Central Maine Power customers.
 A federal ruling found New England power companies were making too much profit on their transmission lines.
 For CMP though, the refunds come as the company is already looking for a rate increase to pay for upgrades, which puts both the company and customers in a tough spot.
 Also read: Westbrook residents discuss Central Maine Power's Greater Portland Transmission Project 
 CMP is seeking an additional $25.6 million a year from customers and wants those higher rates to take effect January 1.
 At the same time, CMP is required to refund customers a portion of the $1.5 billion that federal energy regulators say New England power companies overcharged customers.
 The state public advocate's concern is that customers could start paying higher rates before getting the refunds they are entitled to.
 If you are a Central Maine Power customer, it is still unclear when you will see your federally mandated refund.
 The Office of the Public Advocate wants those refunds distributed starting January 1, the same day customers could see their bills go up.
 In a letter to the Public Utilities Commission, the advocate says CMP's request "makes no sense," arguing customers should not pay more when they are already owed money back.
 Also read: Falmouth residents to discuss the future of CMP's controversial infrastructure plan 
 Federal energy data shows Mainers paid about 61 percent more for electricity than the national average last year.
 The public advocate warns many families are already struggling, writing that "increasing electric rates at this time will exacerbate the extreme burdens faced by Maine citizens as a result of record high spikes in the price of heating fuels."
 To protect ratepayers, the office is recommending two options for CMP:
 Distribute refunds on January 1 and delay the rate hike.
 Lower proposed transmission rates now using an estimated refund, then adjust the charges once the exact amount is finalized.
 The second option is already happening for many electricity customers north of Augusta.
 Also read: Maine Turnpike Authority, Central Maine Power prepare for winter season 
 They use Versant Power, not CMP, and that company is lowering its transmission rates on January 1 to account for the federal refunds, and the public advocate is urging CMP to follow suit.
 Thursday, CBS13 asked CMP why it cannot adopt Versant's plan and whether delaying the rate hike would create any financial or operational challenges.
 So far, we have not heard back.
 CMP and the rest of the New England power companies must distribute refunds to customers by May 20, 2027. It’s unclear when the Public Utilities Commission will make a final decision on CMP's newest transmission rate case.
